A loose idea has arrived, too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** (questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute) one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting: it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic: engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear, with nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes**, carrying execution into the map itself, but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name**: its title. In everything the human reads (narration, the map's Decisions-so-far), refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish; a name wraps its link, but they ride _inside_ the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map`, the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place, its ticket, so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed: they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like: the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index: one line per closed ticket, enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link): <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label, one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship: essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children, the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body; it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** (human in the loop, worked _with_ a human who speaks for themselves) or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a subagent that calls the Skill tool with "research". Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to (an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code) by calling the Skill tool with "prototype". Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation. The default case. Always call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling".
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a _decision_ can be made: nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that _does_ rather than decides, and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war**: the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets, one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination: everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now, _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp, even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope**: it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates (the frontier stops at the destination), so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination (mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution), **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked; a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session**, with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling", to pin down what this map is finding its way to: the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** (the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session), you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create the tickets you can specify now** as child issues of the map, then wire blocking edges in a **second pass** (issues need ids before they can reference each other). Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog: the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a subagent that calls the Skill tool with "research" to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop: charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional**: without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map**: the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.
3. Resolve it. **Zoom as needed**: fetch the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; call the Skill tool for whichever skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling".
4. Record the resolution: post the answer as a **resolution comment**, **close** the issue, and **append a context pointer** to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals that a ticket (this one or another) sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.

- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

1	// Package tui is the two-pane issue navigator behind `drops tui`.
2	//
3	// The left pane lists every live issue in one scope, in the CLI's order; the
4	// right pane is one issue in full. The whole point is that the right pane can
5	// be retargeted without the left cursor moving, so following a relation costs
6	// nothing and loses nothing.
7	//
8	// # Where it sits
9	//
10	// tui imports core, model, render and view. internal/cli builds the command
11	// tree and therefore imports tui, never the reverse (qy3de.3), which is why
12	// everything discovered — the *core.Core, the resolved model.Project, the
13	// comment author, the context — arrives as a parameter rather than being
14	// looked up here. Terminal size is the one exception, and only because
15	// bubbletea delivers it as a message.
16	//
17	// There is deliberately no Store or Reader interface. AGENTS.md's seam rule
18	// puts a discovered FACT behind a parameter and leaves a real subsystem real:
19	// every test in this package runs against real temp SQLite, exactly like the
20	// rest of the repository.
21	//
22	// # What renders what
23	//
24	// The detail pane renders through render.Console into a bytes.Buffer,
25	// unchanged — TTY false, no pager, the measured pane width — and
26	// bubbles/viewport clips the overflow. render.Console.Page truncates nothing,
27	// on purpose, so 43% of open issues emit a line wider than a 37-column pane
28	// (measured for qy3de.3). Those bytes are off-screen and reachable: `h` `l`
29	// scroll to them and `w` soft-wraps instead.
30	//
31	// The left pane's row geometry lives HERE rather than in render, because the
32	// pane deliberately truncates an id and render's doc forbids exactly that. The
33	// truncation primitive is still render's (render.Ellipsis, render.Cols): the
34	// policy differs, the rule does not.
35	//
36	// # Refreshing
37	//
38	// The pane reads the store when it starts, on C and a, after a write, and on
39	// R. It also POLLS, every pollInterval, and the poll's job is noticing rather
40	// than reloading: it reads store_state.write_seq — the counter bumped inside
41	// the same transaction as every replicated write — and puts `stale · R` on the
42	// footer when it has moved. It does not re-read, because this store's common
43	// writer is an agent and a surface that reorders itself under a reader
44	// mid-thought is the thing this package exists to avoid (qy3de.14).
45	//
46	// That split is affordable because the two costs are three orders of magnitude
47	// apart, measured against the 1025-issue corpus: the token is one primary-key
48	// row at 4.2µs, where a whole refresh is 5.5ms scoped and 10.0ms wide, nearly
49	// all of it core.OpenBlockers at 5.24ms.
50	//
51	// reload and refresh are different motions and the difference is navigational,
52	// not about reading. reload is what a scope change does: it clears the follow
53	// stack, because the row set underneath it changed. refresh is what a write
54	// and R do: the stack stands, the filter stands, the cursor rides its tracked
55	// id, and the right pane is REDRAWN rather than reopened — same page, same
56	// scroll position.
57	//
58	// That last part is decided on WHAT IS ON SCREEN and not on which motion the
59	// caller meant. showDetail holds the reader's offsets while the id it is handed
60	// is the one already there and the width it renders into is the width that page
61	// was rendered at, and starts at the top otherwise: a different issue is a page
62	// nobody scrolled, and a different width has reflowed the one they did. So a
63	// refresh whose cursor restore walked onto another issue opens it at line 0
64	// (tc2x5, which is what a `keep` flag believed instead), and `enter`-zoom and a
65	// resize start at the top as they always did. Unchanged is tested on the
66	// rendered text rather than the issue's revision, because a comment is its own
67	// record and would not move the revision of the page it appears on.
68	//
69	// There is deliberately no suppression around any of this. A refresh cannot be
70	// reached from inside a modal or the / prompt — both capture every key before
71	// the keymap sees one — so a guard would be a branch whose control could never
72	// go red, which is precisely the defect AGENTS.md names. The reachability is
73	// asserted by a test instead.
74	//
75	// `r` is NEITHER motion: g7b23's ready-only toggle reads nothing at all. It is
76	// a narrowing, beside `/` — the predicate is blockedBy == 0 over rows the pane
77	// already holds — so it goes through applyFilter, drops the follow stack the
78	// way a filter keystroke does, and survives C and a because every reload
79	// re-derives the visible set through that one function. It is deliberately not
80	// core.Ready: re-asking the store would throw away what the pane's own modes
81	// had put on screen — the closed rows C added, and a deferred issue, which
82	// core.Ready omits. Keeping the predicate local is what leaves the row set as
83	// list's contract under it.
84	//
85	// # Following
86	//
87	// `f` opens a picker over the right pane's relations and `enter` retargets the
88	// pane onto one, pushing onto a stack of ids that `backspace` walks back down;
89	// moving the left cursor clears it. That there is a MODAL at all is forced
90	// rather than chosen: the detail pane is an opaque render.Console buffer, so
91	// the ref lines already on screen are not addressable, and re-listing them
92	// from the core.IssueView is the only way to interact with one without
93	// breaking that opacity (qy3de.6 §3).
94	//
95	// # Getting an id out
96	//
97	// `y` (bvjgn) sends the RIGHT PANE'S id to the system clipboard over OSC 52,
98	// through tea.SetClipboard, which is the whole implementation: no second
99	// process, and this repository ships one static binary. It names the same
100	// issue `x` does, so a follow trail cannot make two keys mean two things.
101	//
102	// OSC 52 is unacknowledged — the terminal takes the sequence or ignores it and
103	// the program cannot tell which — so the footer says what was SENT rather than
104	// what was pasted. It is m.notice and not m.message for the reason qy3de.14
105	// §Q5 gave the stale marker, run the other way: a message costs a pane row,
106	// and the acknowledgement of a keystroke that wrote nothing must die on the

13	// source is every read the pane makes, and the only place it touches core.
14	type source struct {
15		core    *core.Core
16		project model.Project
17	
18		// slugs is the project-key to slug map the project column reads. It is
19		// loaded once: projects are not created while a pane is open, and a
20		// per-refresh reload would be a second store round trip for a table of
21		// fourteen rows.
22		slugs map[model.ProjectKey]string
23	}
24	
25	// rows reads one scope's row set, in the CLI's order — the store's, never
26	// re-sorted — annotated with each issue's open-blocker count.
27	//
28	// Two reads' worth of work, whatever the scope: the issue listing, and one
29	// core.OpenBlockers for the whole store. The blocker map is deliberately
30	// unscoped: a blocker outside the pane's scope still blocks, so a scoped map
31	// would under-report.
32	func (s *source) rows(ctx context.Context, sc scope) ([]row, error) {
33		if s.slugs == nil {
34			projects, err := s.core.Projects(ctx)
35			if err != nil {
36				return nil, err
37			}
38			s.slugs = make(map[model.ProjectKey]string, len(projects))
39			for _, project := range projects {
40				s.slugs[project.Key] = project.Slug
41			}
42		}
43	
44		filter := core.IssueFilter{Statuses: sc.statuses()}
45		if !sc.allProjects {
46			key := s.project.Key
47			filter.Project = &key
48		}
49		issues, err := s.core.Issues(ctx, filter)
50		if err != nil {
51			return nil, err
52		}
53		blockers, err := s.core.OpenBlockers(ctx)
54		if err != nil {
55			return nil, err
56		}
57	
58		rows := make([]row, 0, len(issues))
59		for _, issue := range issues {
60			rows = append(rows, row{
61				id:         issue.ID,
62				project:    s.slugs[issue.ProjectKey],
63				status:     issue.Status,
64				priority:   issue.Priority,
65				title:      issue.Title,
66				tombstoned: issue.Tombstone == model.Tombstoned,
67				blockedBy:  len(blockers[issue.ID]),
68			})
69		}
70		return rows, nil
71	}

73	// issue reads one issue and every relation rendered with it, in core's own
74	// transaction, so a page and the picker over it cannot combine two revisions
75	// of the graph.
76	//
77	// The pane KEEPS this view rather than re-reading for `f`: the relation picker
78	// lists exactly what the page beside it was drawn from, and following a
79	// relation costs no extra read at all.

82	}

88	// straight through. The page truncates nothing at all, which is why the
89	// viewport that clips it has to be scrollable — those bytes are off-screen,
90	// not gone.

112	// it can raise a stale marker for nothing, never miss one.
113	func (s *source) seq(ctx context.Context) (int64, error) {
114		state, err := s.core.State(ctx)

116			return 0, err
117		}

32		title      string
33		tombstoned bool

48	func (s scope) statuses() []model.Status {

60		if needle == "" {

62		}

148	// rowLayout is the left pane's column geometry, measured across the whole row
149	// set exactly once — the way render.measure does it for the CLI.
150	type rowLayout struct {
151		idPad   int
152		projPad int // zero when the project column is off
153		width   int
154	}
155	
156	// measureRows sizes the columns to the widest value present, capped.
157	func measureRows(rows []row, showProject bool, width int) rowLayout {
158		measured := rowLayout{width: width}
159		for _, candidate := range rows {
160			measured.idPad = max(measured.idPad, render.Cols(string(candidate.id)))
161			if showProject {
162				measured.projPad = max(measured.projPad, render.Cols(candidate.project))
163			}
164		}
165		measured.idPad = min(measured.idPad, idCap)
166		measured.projPad = min(measured.projPad, projCap)
167		return measured
168	}
169	
170	// lead is everything left of the title: the CLI's row minus its type column.
171	// Eight columns to say `task` on a pane whose whole job is navigation, with
172	// the detail pane one keypress away, is the cheapest eight columns to spend.
173	//
174	// The glyphs stay render's, so a listing and a page can never disagree about
175	// what a state looks like.
176	func (measured rowLayout) lead(candidate row) string {
177		lead := fmt.Sprintf("%s %-*s P%d",
178			render.StatusMark(candidate.status, candidate.tombstoned),
179			measured.idPad, render.Ellipsis(string(candidate.id), measured.idPad),
180			candidate.priority)
181		if measured.projPad > 0 {
182			lead += fmt.Sprintf(" %-*s", measured.projPad, render.Ellipsis(candidate.project, measured.projPad))
183		}
184		return lead
185	}
186	
187	// marker is how a blocked row says so: four columns, not thirteen.
188	//
189	// qy3de.5 measured the alternatives on the 13 blocked rows of the corpus. At
190	// 80 columns with the project column on, the pane is 38 wide and the lead is
191	// 31, so a 13-column " blocked by N" leaves NEGATIVE room and all 13 rows
192	// render with no title at all. A rule that drops the long form under pressure
193	// was rejected for a different reason: qy3de.4 denied a ready-only key BECAUSE
194	// the row already carries this, and a marker that disappears when the pane is
195	// crowded cannot carry that argument. g7b23 has since given that key out on a
196	// real-use observation, which does not weaken the argument here: the marker is
197	// what tells you the rows `r` would hide are there at all.
198	func marker(candidate row) string {
199		if candidate.blockedBy == 0 {
200			return ""
201		}
202		return fmt.Sprintf(" [%d]", candidate.blockedBy)
203	}
204	
205	// line composes one row.
206	//
207	// The marker is appended AFTER the title is cut, never reserved before it —
208	// euv2e.4 recorded that trap and it is paid for here. The cut itself goes
209	// through render.Ellipsis rather than a second implementation of the same
210	// rule.
211	func (measured rowLayout) line(candidate row) string {
212		lead := measured.lead(candidate)
213		mark := marker(candidate)
214		title := render.Ellipsis(candidate.title, measured.width-render.Cols(lead)-1-render.Cols(mark))
215		if title == "" {
216			return lead + mark
217		}
218		return lead + " " + title + mark
219	}
220	
221	// listBody renders the visible window of rows into exactly height lines,
222	// scrolled so the cursor is on screen.
223	func listBody(rows []row, selected, width, height int, showProject bool, empty string) string {
224		if len(rows) == 0 {
225			return pad(dimStyle.Render(render.Ellipsis(empty, width)), width, height)
226		}
227		measured := measureRows(rows, showProject, width)
228	
229		top := 0
230		if selected >= height {
231			top = selected - height + 1
232		}
233		top = max(0, min(top, len(rows)-height))
234	
235		lines := make([]string, 0, height)
236		for index := top; index < len(rows) && len(lines) < height; index++ {
237			line := measured.line(rows[index])
238			// Padded to the full width before styling, so the cursor's reverse
239			// video covers the whole row rather than stopping at the title.
240			line += strings.Repeat(" ", max(0, width-lipgloss.Width(line)))
241			if index == selected {
242				line = cursorStyle.Render(line)
243			}
244			lines = append(lines, line)
245		}
246		return pad(strings.Join(lines, "\n"), width, height)
247	}

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

Status: measurements are done, and this is the first grilling round for **What reads does the board make, and which does core lack?**

**What I measured** (throwaway benchmark on scratch stores seeded through core; the real store isn't on this machine):

| read | 1,031 issues (1,000 closed) | 10,031 issues (10,000 closed) |
|---|---|---|
| `Issues`, open + in progress, scoped | 0.15ms | 0.15ms |
| `Issues` including closed, scoped | 4.2ms | 54ms |
| `OpenBlockers` | 4.1ms | 48ms |
| `UnblockImpacts` (calls `OpenBlockers` again) | 3.9ms | 47ms |
| `store.Labels()`: every membership, tombstoned included | 0.33ms | 3.2ms |
| Sorting Closed locally by `closed_at` (parses timestamps) | 2.5ms | 36ms |
| **Whole board refresh** (issues + blockers + labels, downstream counts from the same blocker map) | **8.8ms** | **105ms** |

Two things stand out. On the real corpus the board refresh (8.8ms) costs about the same as today's all-projects list (10ms). And `OpenBlockers` grows with the whole store, closed issues included, because it reads full rows for every issue. That already makes the plain list slow on a large store, board or no board.

---

❓ **Q1 - How should the bulk label read look?** Core only has `IssueLabels(id)`. The store's `Labels()` returns every membership, tombstoned ones too, for export. The options:
- (a) A new core read that covers the whole store and returns only live labels, as `map[id][]name` sorted by name. It would be one call per refresh, with no scope, like `OpenBlockers`.
- (b) The same read, limited to one project (or all of them under `a`).
- (c) The same read, limited to a list of ids.

➡️ **(a)**. On a 10k store it costs 3ms, so limiting it saves nothing that matters, and one unscoped call per refresh follows the rule `source.rows` already uses. It needs its own live-only store query instead of filtering the export read, so the tombstone filter lives in one place. Mutation controls: a tombstoned label is left out, and names come back in order.

---

❓ **Q2 - Where do downstream ("unblocks N") counts come from?** Calling `UnblockImpacts` makes a second `OpenBlockers` read on every refresh, which doubles the most expensive read. The options:
- (a) Call `UnblockImpacts` as it is.
- (b) Change core so impacts are computed from a blocker map the caller already has. For example, one core read returns both blocked-by lists and unblock counts, or `UnblockImpacts` takes the map as an argument.
- (c) Count them in the TUI from the `OpenBlockers` map.

➡️ **(b)**. (c) would put a second copy of the "blocks only this one" rule in the TUI, where it could drift from what `drops` reports. (a) spends about 4ms per refresh on the real corpus, and about 47ms at 10k, for nothing.

---

❓ **Q3 - How does Closed get sorted by most recently closed, and does it need a limit?** `tui/doc.go` says rows arrive in the CLI's order and are never re-sorted. The options:
- (a) **Two reads.** The existing open + in-progress read stays as it is. A new core read returns closed issues in scope, ordered `closed_at DESC, id`. The store sorts them, and the no-re-sort rule still holds.
- (b) **One read, sorted locally.** Read everything once and sort the Closed column in the TUI. That is a stated exception to the rule, and it costs 2.5–36ms.
- (c) Like (a), but with a limit, such as the 200 most recently closed, and a heading like `Closed 200 of 1000`.

➡️ **(a) with no limit in v1.** 8.8ms on the real corpus is already inside the refresh budget `doc.go` measures. A limit would change what the map settled as "Closed is always shown", and a separate read makes a limit a one-parameter change later. The 10k case belongs to Q4, not to Closed.

---

❓ **Q4 - Should making `OpenBlockers` scale with the store be ticketed as a core prerequisite?** At 10k closed issues it takes 48ms on every refresh, for the list as well as the board, because it reads every full issue row just to learn each issue's status. Selecting only id, status and tombstone, or joining dependencies to issues in SQL, should make its cost follow the number of edges rather than the store's size. The options:
- (a) Make it a prerequisite ticket for the board.
- (b) Record it in the map's fog and leave it out of v1.
- (c) Rule it out of scope.

➡️ **(b)**. The real corpus is 1,025 issues and the refresh costs 8.8ms there. That doesn't block the board, and the same cost already exists in the list today. The map's "Closed at scale" fog becomes this, sharper: the cost is in `OpenBlockers`, not in loading Closed.

## Destination

A spec for board v1 in `drops tui`, sharp enough to hand to `/to-tickets`, with every core prerequisite it needs identified and ticketed ahead of the TUI work.

## Notes

- Domain: `internal/tui` (read its `doc.go` first — the refresh/poll model, the follow stack, and why the detail pane is opaque), `internal/core` reads and writes, `CONTEXT.md` (**Board column**, Ready/Blocked issue, Deferral).
- Skills: `grilling` + `domain-modeling` for decision tickets; `codebase-design` wherever a new core read or write is shaped; `prototype` for how it looks.
- Reference: bv (beads_viewer) board — `b` opens it; columns Open | In Progress | Blocked | Closed from *stored* status; cards ordered priority then created; 4-line cards (type, P, id, age / title / assignee, blockers, downstream, label count / labels); no card moves.
- Settled while charting (2026-09-15), standing for every ticket:
  - **Columns** are derived (see **Board column** in `CONTEXT.md`): Ready | Blocked | In progress | Closed. An in-progress issue that is blocked stays in In progress with a marker.
  - **Home**: a mode inside `drops tui` that replaces the left pane; the detail pane, follow, `x`, `y`, and the stale marker carry over. Not a separate command.
  - **Card moves** change status. For claims, the close reason, reopening, and refusals, see the decision on moves below.
  - **Order within a column** is the CLI's (priority, newest, id) — no manual ranking. **Closed** is always shown, most recently closed first.
  - **Labels** show on cards, which needs a bulk label read in core (the TUI may not read per card).

## Decisions so far

- [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3): moving into In progress claims when unclaimed, in one new transactional core write; nothing releases; closing uses the `x close` `$EDITOR` flow (empty reason cancels); leaving Closed asks the `reopen` y/N; Ready and Blocked both mean `open`; no revision guard.
- [How does the board fit the navigator's keymap and refresh model?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/5): `B` toggles the board (no flag, not an `Esc` layer), and cursor, filter, `a`, `r`, and follow trail carry over; `tab`/`shift+tab` moves between columns and every existing key keeps its meaning; `m` opens an `open`/`in progress`/`closed` picker; `r` is the same predicate, which empties Blocked; `C` only shows a notice; the cursor rides its id and otherwise moves to the next card; polling is unchanged.
- [How does the board look: columns, cards, and the detail pane?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/2): paged columns — the detail pane keeps 40% (min 38), columns never go under 28 wide and scroll sideways keeping the focused one on screen (1 at 80 cols, 2 at 120, 4 at 200); 3-line cards (mark/P/type/id/age · title · assignee/blocked by/unblocks/labels); columns scroll by card with a `39–41` range in the heading; empty columns show a dim hint. Prototype on branch `prototype/board-look`.

## Not yet specified

- **Contract and test surface.** How the board appears in `docs/cli-contract.md`'s TUI section, and what its boundary and mutation controls look like — keys and moves are decided; sharp once the reads ticket is.
- **Closed at scale.** Always showing Closed means loading every closed issue in scope (most of the store). Whether that needs bounding, lazy loading, or nothing at all hangs on the reads ticket's measurements.

## Out of scope

- **Grouping modes** (bv's `s`: priority or type columns): not v1. No new data is needed, so it's a TUI-only follow-up effort once v1 exists.
- **Manual ordering within a column**: needs a rank column (schema v8) and a sync merge rule for a new replicated record; priority already acts as the rank.
- **Custom workflow stages** (review, QA): a change to the three-status model that readiness and sync depend on; its own effort if ever.
- **A separate `drops board` command**: the board lives inside `drops tui`.
- **A CLI verb for the start-and-claim write** (e.g. `drops start`): it would change the agent-facing CLI contract, which is beyond the board spec. See [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3).
